Local Government (Boundaries) Act (Northern Ireland) 2008 (2008 c. 7)
references.note: Royal Assent 23 May 2008. Section 1 divides Northern Ireland into 11 local government districts, each incorporating the whole or major part of the former districts it names, divided into wards on the recommendations of a Local Government Boundaries Commissioner. Section 1 came into operation for the Commissioner's review one week after Royal Assent, and for all other purposes on 1 Apr 2015 (S.R. 2013 No. 238); the Act also repealed the Local Government (Boundaries) Act (Northern Ireland) 1971.

maps.name: Local Government Districts 1991 (provisional recommendations)
maps.description: The 25 districts the Local Government Boundaries Commissioner provisionally recommended on 3 September 1991. maps.changeNote: Differs from the 1993 districts in Dalriada (Moyle and Ballymoney less the Glens), Ballymena (with the Glens) and the Dromara part of Crossgar townland, which stays in Banbridge (it passed to Lisburn only at the revised stage). maps.changeNote: Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 680 acres of lough north of that line on the County Antrim side of the Victoria Channel now drawn in Belfast North were outside it; the 850 acres north of it on the County Down side now drawn in Belfast East (the Sydenham intake, about 500 acres of it reclaimed land by the early 1960s, and the lough) were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Census of Population 1961, County Borough of Belfast: 18,052 acres including 2,237 acres of tidal water, the land 458 acres more than in 1951, in Victoria Ward, from reclamation; 1951: 15,357 acres of land and 1,223 acres of tidal water. This map shows the seats as first drawn; whether a seat took in the 1958-59 additions with its ward is not settled here.

maps.name: 1969 NI Parliament
provider: Interim Boundary Commission for Northern Ireland
maps.description: The 52 territorial constituencies of the Parliament of Northern Ireland used at the 1969 general election. Forty-two seats are unchanged from 1929 and keep the 1929 lines. Ten seats in Co. Antrim and Co. Down were redrawn, four of them new (Bangor, Lagan Valley, Larkfield and Newtownabbey), by section 2 and Schedule 1 of the Electoral Law Act (Northern Ireland) 1968, which enacted the Interim Boundary Commission for Northern Ireland's 1967 proposals. The redrawn seats are built from whole 1930 district electoral divisions where possible; four divisions split by the proposal (Ballygomartin, Ballyduff, Monkstown and Crawfordsburn) were cut along the Commission's map line, accurate to about 150 m. The Bangor seat follows the borough as extended on 1 April 1967, plus Groomsport. Checked against Schedule 1 of the Act: the list of seats and their names agree (the Act spells Bannside 'Bann Side'), and the composition of Bann Side, South Antrim, Bangor, Lagan Valley, Mid Down and North Down matches the Act. Antrim, Carrick, Larkfield and Newtownabbey are defined in the Act by divisions of Lisburn Rural District created in 1963 (Suffolk, Andersonstown, Ardmore, Ballygammon, Finaghy, Ladybrook, Upper Malone) and by wards of Newtownabbey Urban District, for which no maps are held, so their lines through the former Belfast Rural District follow the Commission's map and are not confirmed. The Commission's population and electorate figures for the redrawn seats are included. The Queen's University seats, abolished by the same Act, had no territory and are not shown.

maps.changeNote: Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 679 acres of lough north of that line on the County Antrim side of the Victoria Channel now drawn in Belfast Duncairn were outside it; the 834 acres north of it on the County Down side now drawn in Belfast Victoria (the Sydenham intake, about 500 acres of it reclaimed land by the early 1960s, and the lough) were outside it; the 20 acres of lough north of the Inner Lighthouse now drawn in Belfast Pottinger were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Census of Population 1961, County Borough of Belfast: 18,052 acres including 2,237 acres of tidal water, the land 458 acres more than in 1951, in Victoria Ward, from reclamation; 1951: 15,357 acres of land and 1,223 acres of tidal water. This map shows the seats as first drawn; whether a seat took in the 1958-59 additions with its ward is not settled here.

references.note: OSNI Baronies and Parishes maps obtained via FOI request to Mapping.Helpdesk@finance-ni.gov.uk, who commented as follows: "The Parish and Baronies dataset was created in 2007 based on the existing Townlands dataset combined with NISRA data for a specific project. While it was originally envisaged that the dataset would be released as an additional OSNI product for public supply, it proved difficult to verify the exact townlands making up parishes due to conflicts within source material. The data was developed to a state that was fit-for-purpose at the time, however, OSNI was unable to fully QA the product and so was not considered to be at a sufficient standard to add to our product catalogue. As customers enquired after the dataset, as a goodwill gesture, we agreed to share it on request, with the understanding that it is not an official product and so we could not stand over its accuracy or completeness. For the same reason, there is no documentation or analysis of the data to support it. Therefore, the only additional information we can provide you with is what we have observed from our own review of the data: there are topographical errors, such as sliver polygons, missing attribution and additional fields that could be cleansed out if desired."

maps.changeNote: Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 680 acres of lough north of that line on the County Antrim side of the Victoria Channel now drawn in Belfast North were outside it; the 850 acres north of it on the County Down side now drawn in Belfast East (the Sydenham intake, about 500 acres of it reclaimed land by the early 1960s, and the lough) were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Census of Population 1961, County Borough of Belfast: 18,052 acres including 2,237 acres of tidal water, the land 458 acres more than in 1951, in Victoria Ward, from reclamation; 1951: 15,357 acres of land and 1,223 acres of tidal water.

Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 1533 acres beyond that line now drawn in Belfast County Borough (the Sydenham intake and the lough; 6.2 km2) were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Newcastle UD is one DED (Newcastle) with two wards, as the 1926 Census lists it. Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 679 acres of lough north of that line on the County Antrim side of the Victoria Channel now drawn in Duncairn Ward were outside it; the 854 acres north of it on the County Down side now drawn in Victoria Ward (the Sydenham intake, about 500 acres of it reclaimed land by the early 1960s, and the lough) were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Census of Population 1961, County Borough of Belfast: 18,052 acres including 2,237 acres of tidal water, the land 458 acres more than in 1951, in Victoria Ward, from reclamation; 1951: 15,357 acres of land and 1,223 acres of tidal water.

maps.name: District Electoral Divisions 3 May 1921
maps.description: Northern Ireland District Electoral Divisions as at 3 May 1921. A modified version of the 1911 DEDs/wards map, capturing the three changes made in the six counties between 1911 and partition: the DED of Gortahurk ceded six townlands to Cuilcagh (both in Fermanagh), and Portstewart and Ballycastle each split their DED into urban and rural. Some errors with the map were also fixed (Rich Hill/Aghory, Enagh/"Ballymoney Rural", Derryaghy/"Lambeg", Lissue/Lisburn Urban, Larne, Bangor, Newtownards, Dungannon, Omagh) using the 1911 census reports as a source.

maps.boundaryOrdersSource: Local Government Board for Ireland orders (Dublin Gazette), transcribed by Phelim Birch
maps.changeNote: Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. Bdy.") on the OSNI six-inch County Down sheet 4, Edition 5 (revised 1931), and County Antrim sheet 57, Edition 5 (revised 1931); the same line is on Down sheet 4 Edition 3 (1902) and Edition 4 (1920-21) and Antrim sheet 57 Editions 3-4 (1901-02). The county borough lay south and west of that line: the 679 acres of lough north of that line on the County Antrim side of the Victoria Channel now drawn in Duncairn Ward were outside it; the 854 acres north of it on the County Down side now drawn in Victoria Ward (the Sydenham intake, about 500 acres of it reclaimed land by the early 1960s, and the lough) were outside it. These areas were added to Belfast by Orders in Council under section 11 of the Boundary Survey (Ireland) Act 1854: S.R.&O. 1957 No. 189 (with No. 188 for County Down), made 29 Aug 1957, in force 1 Mar 1958 (Belfast Gazette issue 1889, 6 Sep 1957, pp. 243-244), and the Belfast order of 9 Feb 1959, in force 1 Apr 1959 (Belfast Gazette issue 1965, 20 Feb 1959, p. 66; issue 1979, 29 May 1959, p. 185), whose added area "consists of reclaimed lands at Sydenham" (issue 2070, 24 Feb 1961, p. 58). Census of Population 1961, County Borough of Belfast: 18,052 acres including 2,237 acres of tidal water, the land 458 acres more than in 1951, in Victoria Ward, from reclamation; 1951: 15,357 acres of land and 1,223 acres of tidal water.

references.label: OSNI Largescale Baronies — FlatGeobuf download
references.note: OSNI Baronies and Parishes maps obtained via FOI request to Mapping.Helpdesk@finance-ni.gov.uk, who commented as follows: "The Parish and Baronies dataset was created in 2007 based on the existing Townlands dataset combined with NISRA data for a specific project. While it was originally envisaged that the dataset would be released as an additional OSNI product for public supply, it proved difficult to verify the exact townlands making up parishes due to conflicts within source material. The data was developed to a state that was fit-for-purpose at the time, however, OSNI was unable to fully QA the product and so was not considered to be at a sufficient standard to add to our product catalogue. As customers enquired after the dataset, as a goodwill gesture, we agreed to share it on request, with the understanding that it is not an official product and so we could not stand over its accuracy or completeness. For the same reason, there is no documentation or analysis of the data to support it. Therefore, the only additional information we can provide you with is what we have observed from our own review of the data: there are topographical errors, such as sliver polygons, missing attribution and additional fields that could be cleansed out if desired."

variants.label: By geological age (IUGS)
variants.description: Bedrock geology coloured by geological period / era using the IUGS / International Commission on Stratigraphy palette (the textbook age-coloured map). Coarser than the formation view but immediately legible — Carboniferous teal, Cretaceous green, Palaeogene orange, etc.

maps.name: Bedrock Geology 1:250,000 (Lines)
maps.description: Faults, bedrock boundaries, fold axial traces, dykes and bedrock lineaments across Northern Ireland at 1:250,000 scale.

maps.name: Superficial Geology 1:250,000
maps.description: Superficial (Quaternary) deposits — glacial till, alluvium, peat, raised beach and other surface materials — mapped at 1:250,000 scale.

variants.label: By deposit type (BGS palette)
variants.description: Quaternary superficial deposits coloured by deposit-type using the official BGS / GSNI 1:250K palette from the published QGIS style file. ALLUVIUM yellow, TILL pale cyan, PEAT brown, GLACIAL SAND AND GRAVEL pink — the colours used in the BGS Geology of Britain Viewer.

variants.label: By deposit type (conventional earth-tones)
variants.description: Quaternary superficial deposits coloured using the conventional textbook earth-tone palette (TILL brown, ALLUVIUM yellow, BLOWN SAND cream) rather than the BGS-pink convention.

maps.name: Mineral Resources (Northern Ireland)
maps.description: Mapped surface extent of commercially significant mineral resources — coal, lignite, sand and gravel, limestone, sandstone, peat, clay, igneous rock and others — merged into one layer attributed by mineral_type.

references.label: GSNI Northern Ireland Mineral Resources — Open Data NI
PDF versions of NI Mineral Maps (British Geological Survey)
references.note: External BGS index page listing PDF mineral resource maps for Northern Ireland.

maps.name: Tellus Stream Sediments (Regional XRF)
maps.description: Regional stream-sediment samples collected under the Tellus survey, analysed by XRF for major and trace elements. Approximately 5,800 sample points across Northern Ireland.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Regional Stream Sediments — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Stream Waters (Regional ICP)
maps.description: Regional stream-water samples collected under the Tellus survey, analysed by ICP-MS for dissolved elements. Approximately 5,900 sample points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Regional Stream Waters — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Rural Soil Survey (A Soils, XRF)
maps.description: Topsoil ("A horizon") samples collected on a 2 km grid across rural Northern Ireland under the Tellus survey and analysed by XRF. Approximately 6,860 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Rural Soil Survey — Open Data NI

maps.name: GSNI Core and Cuttings Register
maps.description: Registered borehole cores and cuttings held by the Geological Survey of Northern Ireland. Only records with geographic coordinates are shown on the map (~140 of ~345).

references.label: Spreadsheet of Core and Cuttings held by GSNI — Open Data NI

maps.name: OSNI Map Sheet Coverage Grid — 1:10,000
maps.description: Polygonal overlay of Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland 1:10,000-scale printed-map tile footprints, labelled by sheet name. Useful for locating which historic / current OSNI sheet covers a site.

maps.name: OSNI Map Sheet Coverage Grid — 1:50,000
maps.description: Polygonal overlay of OSNI 1:50,000-scale printed-map tile footprints, labelled by tile identifier — the coarser complement to the 1:10K coverage grid.

maps.name: OSNI Benchmarks (Height Reference Points)
maps.description: Historic OSNI benchmarks — small brass plates or chiselled grooves set into permanent features (bridges, walls, milestones) whose heights above Ordnance Datum were precisely determined by levelling surveys. Used by surveyors as known reference points before GPS. ~10,000 points across Northern Ireland, each attributed with its height in metres.

maps.name: Tellus Stream Sediments (Regional XRF — Set 2)
maps.description: Second set of regional stream-sediment samples (Tellus survey), analysed by XRF for an additional suite of major and trace elements beyond the Set 1 panel. ~5,870 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Regional Stream Sediments — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Stream Sediments (Gold and Platinum Group Elements)
maps.description: Tellus stream-sediment samples assayed specifically for gold (Au) and platinum group elements (PGE — Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Os, Ir). ~5,690 sample points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Regional Stream Sediments — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Stream Sediments (Boron)
maps.description: Tellus stream-sediment samples specifically analysed for boron, which requires a separate analytical method from the main XRF panel. ~5,840 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Regional Stream Sediments — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Rural Soil (A Horizon — Aqua Regia Digest)
maps.description: A-horizon (topsoil) samples from the Tellus rural soil survey digested with aqua regia and analysed for the trace/heavy metal elements that resist XRF. Complements the A-horizon XRF layer. ~6,870 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Rural Soil Survey — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Rural Soil (S Horizon — Aqua Regia Digest)
maps.description: S-horizon (subsoil) samples from the Tellus rural soil survey, aqua regia digest. The deeper soil samples — useful for distinguishing surface anthropogenic contamination from underlying geology. ~6,870 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Rural Soil Survey — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Rural Soil (S Horizon — Near-Total Digest)
maps.description: S-horizon (subsoil) samples digested with HF-HClO4-HNO3 ("near total") and analysed by ICP-MS — a more aggressive extraction than aqua regia, recovering more of the silicate-bound element pool. ~6,870 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Rural Soil Survey — Open Data NI

maps.name: Tellus Rural Soil (S Horizon — Fire Assay for Au and PGE)
maps.description: S-horizon subsoil samples subjected to fire assay specifically to recover gold (Au) and platinum group elements. The classical mineral-prospecting technique applied across the Tellus survey grid. ~6,850 points.

references.label: GSNI Tellus Rural Soil Survey — Open Data NI

maps.name: OSNI Éire Thuaidh — Irish-Translated Map

maps.name: OSNI Mid-Scale Raster — 1:10,000
maps.description: Topographic raster cartography at 1:10,000 scale across all of Northern Ireland — a 292-sheet mosaic of OSNI base-map tiles. Useful background context for site-level work; shows roads, settlements, contours and named features. Served as XYZ tiles at zoom 8–15.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Mid Scale Raster

maps.name: OSNI StreetMaps — Town Sheets
maps.description: Detailed printed street-map sheets for 109 towns and villages across Northern Ireland — 0.85 m/pixel native resolution showing individual streets, building outlines, and town features. maps.name: OSNI 1:1M Thematic — County Boundaries
maps.description: Small-scale (1:1,000,000) printed thematic map of Northern Ireland showing the historic six-county boundaries against a base outline. Designed as a wall-poster reference — re-tiled here as an interactive overlay at zoom 6–11.

maps.name: OSNI 1:1M Thematic — Infrastructure
maps.description: Small-scale (1:1,000,000) thematic map showing major roads, railways, ports, airports, and other transport infrastructure across Northern Ireland. Re-tiled as an interactive overlay at zoom 6–11.

maps.name: OSNI 1:1M Thematic — Locations
maps.description: Small-scale (1:1,000,000) thematic map labelling major settlements and locations across Northern Ireland. Re-tiled as an interactive overlay at zoom 6–11.

maps.name: OSNI 1:1M Thematic — Natural Environment
maps.description: Small-scale (1:1,000,000) thematic map of Northern Ireland’s natural environment — drainage, lakes, mountains, and broad land cover. Re-tiled as an interactive overlay at zoom 6–11.

maps.name: OSNI 1:1M Thematic — Parliamentary Boundaries
maps.description: Small-scale (1:1,000,000) thematic map showing Northern Ireland’s Westminster parliamentary constituency boundaries. Re-tiled as an interactive overlay at zoom 6–11.

maps.description: Long-term chemistry time-series from NI rivers, 1990–2018, broken down by 14 individual parameters (pH, dissolved oxygen, BOD, ammonia, nitrate, nitrite, dissolved iron, suspended solids, plus extended set: alkalinity, conductivity, dissolved copper, dissolved zinc, soluble phosphorus). maps.name: Tellus Magnetic — Total Magnetic Intensity (residual)
maps.description: Residual total magnetic intensity (TMI) from the GSNI Tellus airborne survey — variations in the Earth's magnetic field caused by buried magnetic minerals (chiefly magnetite). High-magnetic anomalies trace mafic/ultramafic intrusions, basaltic flows, and iron-bearing sedimentary basins; magnetic lows mark sedimentary basins and demagnetised alteration zones. 35m grid spacing, ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

maps.name: Tellus Magnetic — Reduction-to-Pole (RTP)
maps.description: TMI corrected by reduction-to-pole, which compensates for the dipolar shape of magnetic anomalies caused by NI's inclined magnetic field. RTP places the peak directly above the source body, simplifying interpretation. ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

maps.name: Tellus Magnetic — RTP Tilt Derivative
maps.description: Tilt derivative of the RTP magnetic field — an edge-detection filter that highlights the boundaries of magnetic source bodies regardless of their amplitude. Excellent for tracing dykes, faults, and contacts. ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

maps.name: Tellus Electromagnetic — 3 kHz Apparent Conductivity
maps.description: Apparent ground conductivity at 3 kHz from the Tellus airborne EM survey — penetrates ~50–150 m, mapping conductive saline groundwater, clay-rich soils, mineralised zones, and pollution plumes. Viridis colormap (low = purple, high = yellow), -2σ to +4σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Electromagnetic Grids

maps.name: Tellus Electromagnetic — 14 kHz Apparent Conductivity
maps.description: Apparent ground conductivity at 14 kHz — shallower depth (~10–30 m) than the 3 kHz channel, more sensitive to surface and near-surface conductors. Useful for soil moisture, near-surface alteration, and thin clay layers. Viridis colormap, -2σ to +4σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Electromagnetic Grids

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — Potassium (K %)
maps.description: Surface potassium concentration from natural gamma-ray emissions. Highlights granites and other felsic intrusions (potassium-rich), alkaline volcanics, and certain sedimentary horizons. Inferno colormap (dark = low, bright = high), ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — Uranium-Equivalent (eU ppm)
maps.description: Uranium-equivalent concentration from the 1.76 MeV bismuth-214 daughter peak. Highlights uranium-bearing granites, organic-rich shales, phosphatic horizons, and mineralised zones. Viridis colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — Thorium-Equivalent (eTh ppm)
maps.description: Thorium-equivalent concentration from the 2.61 MeV thallium-208 daughter peak. Often correlates with heavy minerals (monazite, zircon) in placer deposits and resistate sediments. Rainbow colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — Total Counts (gamma)
maps.description: Total gamma-ray count rate — a summed proxy for combined K, U, Th, and other radionuclide activity. Useful for identifying overall radiometric "hot" zones before decomposing into individual channels. Inferno colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — K/Th/U Ternary RGB
maps.description: The iconic radiometric ternary composite — K mapped to red, Th to green, U to blue. Reds = potassic (granite, certain volcanics); greens = thorium-rich (resistate sediments, heavy minerals); blues = uranium-rich (organic shales, mineralisation); whites/pale = high in all three; blacks = low overall. The most interpretively powerful single radiometric view. Each band stretched independently to mean ± 2σ.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

maps.name: OSNI Historical Six-Inch Maps — Edition 1 (1829–1835)
maps.description: The original Six-Inch-to-One-Mile County Series — the first complete topographic survey of Ireland, produced 1829–1835 by the Ordnance Survey. 308 historical map sheets covering all six Northern Ireland counties (Antrim, Armagh, Derry/Londonderry, Down, Fermanagh, Tyrone), engraved at a scale where every individual building, road, field boundary, and town feature is shown. Mosaicked and re-tiled here at 4 m/pixel for interactive viewing on the catalogue map. For pixel-level detail, download the original sheet TIFs from the per-county packages linked below.

maps.name: Tellus Magnetic — raw airborne flight-line data
maps.description: Raw magnetometer readings along each Tellus survey flight line — the original point measurements that the gridded "Tellus Magnetic" products on this site are derived from. Typically ~250 m line spacing with samples every ~7 m. Useful only if you want to re-grid with custom parameters or interrogate noise; for a map-style view use the gridded TMI / RTP / RTP-Tilt cards in this category.

maps.name: Tellus Electromagnetic — raw airborne flight-line data
maps.description: Raw multi-frequency airborne EM coil readings along each Tellus flight line — the original point measurements behind the gridded conductivity products. Frequencies 912 Hz, 3 kHz, 11.9 kHz, and 24.5 kHz at the same line/sample spacing as the magnetic data.

maps.name: Tellus Radiometric — raw airborne flight-line data

maps.name: Agricultural Critical Risk Areas (DAERA)
maps.description: DAERA classification of land parcels by their relative risk of contributing diffuse agricultural pollution to receiving waters. Each parcel is scored 0–1 (`riskscore2`) by combining slope, hydrological connectivity, soil characteristics, rainfall, river-buffer proximity and land-use rules. Companion to the Network Contribution datasets — the polygon equivalent of the per-river-basin SciMAP score.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Agricultural Critical Risk Areas

maps.name: DAERA Network Contribution — SciMAP modelled pollution scores by river basin (26 catchments)
maps.description: Per-river-basin pollution-contribution scores from the SciMAP hydrological model (CEH Land Cover 2007 + Met Office rainfall + 5 m DTM), rasterised at 25 m and rendered as a Web Mercator tile pyramid coloured on inferno (low → high contribution). Raw GRIDCODE values of 58–100 stretch the inferno ramp from dark purple to pale yellow. Each parcel of land is scored for how much sediment / nutrient pollution its upstream catchment contributes to receiving waters. 26 catchment datasets were rasterised individually, mosaicked, and re-projected; per-catchment download links remain in sourceDownloads for the raw vector data.

references.label: DAERA Open Data Hub — Network Contribution datasets

Modified version of District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1950. In 1950, the new DED of Limerick Rural was formed out of parts of Limerick North Rural and Limerick South Rural due to the forthcoming expansion of Limerick county borough. Also relevant is the renaming of the following DEDs between 1936 Census Reports Volume 1 (published 1938) and 1946 Census Reports Volume 1 (published 1949): Edgeworthstown to Meathas Truim (Longford), Drumcondra to Drumconrath (Meath), Philipstown to Daingean (Offaly), Charleville to Rathluirc (Cork), Shanballymore to Shanballymore Town (Cork)

maps.name: District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1931
maps.description: Republic of Ireland District Electoral Divisions/Wards as at 1931-04-01, assembled from Connacht (= 1919 boundaries), Leinster 1931, Munster (= 1921 boundaries), Ulster (= 1921 boundaries). Modified version of District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1936. In 1936, Dublin county borough’s wards were modified. 14 of the existing 20 wards remained the same, 2 of them were split in 2 and the other 4 were expanded. The DEDs of Pembroke East, Pembroke West (previously wards of Pembroke Township) and Rathmines and Rathgar West (previously a ward of Rathmines & Rathgar Township) were converted into wards. The DED of Rathmines and Rathgar East (previously a ward of Rathmines and Rathgar Township) was converted into a ward and expanded. With 7 brand new wards being formed, the total number of wards was increased to 33. The 2 DEDs of Glasnevin Rural and Donnybrook were fully absorbed while the 7 DEDs of Castleknock, Drumcondra Rural, Finglas, Howth Rural, Palmerston, Rathfarnham and Terenure were reduced in size.

maps.name: Poor Law Unions 2 Apr 1911
maps.description: The 158 Poor Law Unions of Ireland at the census of 2 Apr 1911: 112 in one county, 38 in two and 8 in three. Each union is built by grouping the 3,673 District Electoral Divisions of the 1911 census by the union they were in, from the county districts in each county volume's Table VI and the DED numbers in Table VII (which runs union by union). The DED map is Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's (Leinster 29 Apr 1910, Connacht and Munster 1907, Ulster as on census day). Every union's DED areas add up to the acreage printed in the 1911 General Report Table 51 (152 of 158 within 0.01%), and its DED populations to the printed population. Each union carries its census acreage and population; quote census_acres rather than the map area, which takes in large lakes and estuaries the census leaves out. The King's County DEDs are placed from Table VI of the 1911 King's County volume.
maps.changeNote: Since 1901: Tulla Union was dissolved and its area added to Scarriff Union, and part of Lisheen DED (Killadysert Union) was added to Clareabbey DED (Ennis Union), about 1,087 acres. Corrected 1 Nov 2026: four King's County DEDs were in the wrong union and now follow the 1911 King's County volume (Ballycumber and Roscomroe to Birr, Ballincor to Roscrea, Killooly to Tullamore), and the gaps over Finglas, Castleknock and Drumcondra Rural (North Dublin) and Faithlegg (Waterford), about 100 km2, are filled.

maps.name: Poor Law Unions 31 Mar 1901
maps.description: The 159 Poor Law Unions of Ireland at the census of 31 Mar 1901, the 1911 unions together with Tulla. They are built by grouping Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's District Electoral Divisions by the union each belonged to in the 1901 census county volumes (Table VI county districts and Table VII, arranged by union). No DED map earlier than 1907 exists, so the lines are those of 1907-1912; DEDs formed after 1901 take the union of the division they were split from. The one known change between unions, part of Lisheen DED (Killadysert) to Clareabbey (Ennis), is drawn on its later line. King's County and Queen's County are placed from their own 1901 volumes. The 1901 Limerick volume is not held, so Limerick follows the 1911 lists, and the population is left blank for the eight unions with parts there (Croom, Kilmallock, Limerick, Listowel, Mitchelstown, Newcastle, Rathkeale and Tipperary).
maps.changeNote: Since 30 Sep 1891: no union was formed or dissolved, so the 159 unions are those of Poor Law Unions 30 Sep 1891, but about 21 DEDs changed union in 1898-99 (among them Cranemore and Clonegall, which joined Carlow Union), and Kyle South had moved from Urlingford to Roscrea by 1901. Glin Union had been dissolved on 30 Sep 1891, its divisions going to Listowel and Rathkeale. Corrected 1 Nov 2026: four King's County DEDs now follow the 1901 King's County volume (Ballycumber and Roscomroe to Birr, Ballincor to Roscrea, Killooly to Tullamore); the gaps over Finglas, Castleknock and Drumcondra Rural (North Dublin) and Faithlegg (Waterford), about 100 km2, are filled; and the census acreage, which had been double-counted in 23 unions, is now the sum of the 1901 Table VI DED areas.

maps.name: Poor Law Unions 30 Mar 1851
maps.description: The 163 Poor Law Unions of Ireland at the census of 30 Mar 1851, as the 1851 county reports list them under 'Poor Law Unions and Electoral Divisions'. The same unions stood from the declaration of Castletowndelvin on 9 Aug 1850, the last of the 33 unions formed in 1848-50, until Newport was dissolved on 30 Sep 1885. No map of the 1851 electoral divisions exists, so each union is drawn as the 1907-12 District Electoral Divisions (Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's maps) that cover its 1851 divisions, matched by name from hand transcriptions of the printed tables; a division printed as 'part of' is given whole to one union, and town divisions redrawn by 1891 are matched by name. Each union carries its land area (land_acres: the map area less large lakes and tideway, which the census also leaves out), the sum of its printed county-part acreages (census_acres), the difference (pct_diff) and a confidence grade. Of the 157 unions that can be checked, 146 agree within 1% and 153 within 2% (median 0.11%); Belfast (+8.4%, reclaimed foreshore inside the later city wards), Wexford (+4.8%, reclaimed slobs), Londonderry (+4.0%, divisions redrawn round Derry, Coleraine and Limavady) and Donegal (-2.8%, Lough Eask counted by the census) are further out. The King's County divisions are from the 1851 King's County report. Six unions are graded unchecked: the six Dublin unions (Balrothery, Celbridge, Dunshaughlin, North Dublin, Rathdown and South Dublin), which follow the 1891 tables because the CSO file labelled 1851 Dublin is in fact the Queen's County report (so Queen's County is checked and Dublin is not). The map is simplified for display by a coverage simplification of the division map, so neighbouring unions keep common edges (95% of divisions lie within 10 m of the full lines); the full-resolution file is among the downloads.
maps.changeNote: Earliest edition. Scariff, Corofin, Ballyvaghan, Castletownbere and Borrisokane already have their divisions in the 1851 tables, though workhouses.org.uk dates them 1852-53. The 130 unions before 1848 are not drawn: the census gives no union tables for them. Corrected 1 Nov 2026: the King's County divisions, approximated until the 1851 King's County report was read, now follow it (Ballaghassaan to Edenderry, O'Dempsey to Mountmellick, Roscomroe to Parsonstown, Ballincor to Roscrea, Killooly to Tullamore).

maps.description: The 162 Poor Law Unions of Ireland after Newport Union was dissolved into Westport on 30 Sep 1885, until Donaghmore was dissolved on 30 Sep 1886. Derived from the 5 Apr 1891 map with Gortin and Donaghmore given back the divisions they held in 1851. Divisions that moved between unions at dates not established between 1851 and 1891 are drawn as in 1891; most of those moves were of parts of divisions (Knockatooan, Tullaghmelan, Burtonhall, the Clare part of Gort, Holycross, Longfordpass, Cloonbur, Kilmovee, Ballymoe, Cullenwaine), which the 1907-12 division map cannot show. See Poor Law Unions 5 Apr 1891 for the method and the checks against the printed areas, which apply here. The map is simplified for display by a coverage simplification of the division map, so neighbouring unions keep common edges (95% of divisions lie within 10 m of the full lines); the full-resolution file is among the downloads.

maps.name: Poor Law Unions 5 Apr 1891
maps.description: The 160 Poor Law Unions of Ireland at the census of 5 Apr 1891, as Table VI of each 1891 county report lists them. The same unions stood from the dissolution of Gortin on 1 Apr 1889 until Glin was dissolved on 30 Sep 1891. Each union is drawn as the 1907-12 District Electoral Divisions (Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's maps) that cover its 1891 divisions, matched by name from hand transcriptions of the printed tables (Mayo and Sligo from OCR, checked by hand). Each union carries its land area (land_acres: the map area less large lakes and tideway, which the census also leaves out), the sum of its printed county-part acreages (census_acres), the difference (pct_diff) and a confidence grade. All 160 unions can be checked: 156 agree within 1% (142 within 0.5%; median 0.08%); Belfast (+6.7%, reclaimed foreshore inside the later city wards), Wexford (+4.8%, reclaimed slobs), Donegal (-3.0%, Lough Eask counted by the census) and Glenties (+1.8%) are further out. The King's County and Queen's County divisions are from Table VI of their own 1891 reports. Carlow agrees exactly: its printed 1891 total of 185,155 acres matches the map; the 199,998 acres of 1911 include Cranemore and Clonegall, which joined the union between 1891 and 1901. The map is simplified for display by a coverage simplification of the division map, so neighbouring unions keep common edges (95% of divisions lie within 10 m of the full lines); the full-resolution file is among the downloads.

maps.name: Poor Law Unions 1 Apr 1924
maps.description: The 27 Poor Law Unions of Northern Ireland from 1 Apr 1924 until the boards of guardians' functions passed to the county welfare and health authorities on 5 Jul 1948; every board was abolished on 30 Sep 1948. Each union is the dissolution of its district electoral divisions on Civgraph's 1926 DED map (Paddy Matthews), placed in their unions by the 1926 Census Topographical Index. The only change from 1921 is the Ardkeen, Portaferry and Quintin area, moved from Downpatrick to Newtownards Union; the 1937 Census records no union changes in 1926-37, the district changes of 1937-48 each fell inside one union, and the Belfast Gazette to 1948 has no order altering a union. Each union carries its 1926 and 1937 census acreage and population; with the large loughs taken out the map areas agree with the census acreages to a median of 0.2%. After 1948 the unions remained as superintendent registrars' districts.

maps.description: The 27 Poor Law Unions in the six counties from 1 Apr 1921, a month before partition, until 31 Mar 1924. maps.name: Dispensary Districts 1 Jan 1929
maps.description: The 178 dispensary districts of Northern Ireland from 1 Jan 1929, when Londonderry Urban No. 3 was formed out of No. 2, until the dispensary service passed to the Northern Ireland General Health Services Board on the appointed day of the Health Services Act (NI) 1948, 5 Jul 1948. Each district is a group of the old (pre-1923) electoral divisions on Civgraph's 3 May 1921 DED map (Paddy Matthews, with Phelim Birch's corrections), because the Ministry of Home Affairs ordered in 1925 that dispensary districts stay as they were before the 1923 reconstitution of the divisions. The district of each old division is the one its townlands carry in the 1926 Census Topographical Index, checked against the district lists of the 1926 county volumes (Table 4) and the order of the 1911 Census Table VI. Ten old divisions were shared between districts; these are split on OSNI townland lines (Brownlows Derry, Ballygomartin, Ballysillan, Monkstown, Ardclinis, Beardiville, Portrush Rural, Kilkeel, Newry Rural and Drumnakilly). The 16 Belfast urban districts and the Londonderry urban districts other than Waterside cross ward lines along streets, so each county borough's urban districts are shown as one undivided area. With the large loughs taken out, 93 of the 97 county parts whose 1926 printed area could be read agree within 2% (median 0.06%); each district carries its grade and the reason for it (confidence, confidence_reason). Dispensary districts were also the registrars' districts for births, deaths and marriages. No change between 1929 and 1948 has been found: the 1937 Census lists none after 1929, and no order appears in the Belfast Gazette to 1948.

maps.name: Dispensary Districts 1 Apr 1921
maps.description: The 177 dispensary districts in the six counties from 1 Apr 1921, when the unions that crossed the new border were reorganised, until 31 Mar 1924. The Belleek, Clones No. 2 and Crossmaglen areas passed with their districts to the Irvinestown, Lisnaskea and Newry Unions, and the Cavan districts of Enniskillen Union and the Donegal districts of Londonderry and Strabane Unions were taken out. Each district is a group of the old (pre-1923) electoral divisions on Civgraph's 3 May 1921 DED map (Paddy Matthews, with Phelim Birch's corrections), because the Ministry of Home Affairs ordered in 1925 that dispensary districts stay as they were before the 1923 reconstitution of the divisions. The district of each old division is the one its townlands carry in the 1926 Census Topographical Index, checked against the district lists of the 1926 county volumes (Table 4) and the order of the 1911 Census Table VI. Ten old divisions were shared between districts; these are split on OSNI townland lines (Brownlows Derry, Ballygomartin, Ballysillan, Monkstown, Ardclinis, Beardiville, Portrush Rural, Kilkeel, Newry Rural and Drumnakilly). The 16 Belfast urban districts and the Londonderry urban districts other than Waterside cross ward lines along streets, so each county borough's urban districts are shown as one undivided area. With the large loughs taken out, 93 of the 97 county parts whose 1926 printed area could be read agree within 2% (median 0.06%); each district carries its grade and the reason for it (confidence, confidence_reason). Dispensary districts were also the registrars' districts for births, deaths and marriages. No dispensary district change between 1921 and 1926 is recorded (the 1926 General Report does not list them), so the 1926 districts are carried back; Portaferry is in Downpatrick Union.
maps.changeNote: Since partition: the unions crossing the new border were reorganised (1 Apr 1921); their Northern Ireland dispensary districts joined the Irvinestown, Lisnaskea and Newry Unions.

maps.name: Rural and Urban Districts 2 Apr 1911
maps.description: The 309 county districts of Ireland on census day, 2 Apr 1911: rural districts (each the part of one poor law union in one administrative county), urban districts and the six county boroughs. Each is built by dissolving the 3,673 District Electoral Divisions of the 1911 census by the county district it is printed under in Table VI of the 1911 county volumes. Rural districts carry the names in force in 1911, with the former numbered name (for example Aghalee, formerly Lurgan No. 3) where the district was renamed about 1901-02, and their union. Each district carries its census acreage (the sum of its printed DED areas) and population; the map areas agree with them to a median of 0.2%, apart from districts on large lakes and estuaries, which the census leaves out.
maps.changeNote: Since 1901: 41 rural districts renamed about 1901-02 (the former names are in the "formerly" field); Ballyclare, Keady, Macroom, Mallow, Donaghadee, Newcastle (Down) and Arklow are urban districts; Tulla Union was merged into Scarriff, but Tulla rural district continued. King's County's districts are from Table VI of its 1911 volume (read 1 Nov 2026): Birr No. 1, Clonygowan, Edenderry No. 1, Roscrea No. 2 and Tullamore (formerly Tullamore No. 1) rural districts and Birr and Tullamore urban districts, each with its printed acreage and population; Ballycumber and Roscomroe are in Birr No. 1, Ballincor in Roscrea No. 2 and Killooly in Tullamore. Belfast is drawn as it was before 1958. Across Belfast Lough the boundary ran in a straight line from the Antrim shore south of Greencastle to the Inner Lighthouse at the tip of the East Twin, and from there in a straight line to the railway at Tillysburn, as shown ("Co. Boro. maps.name: Dispensary Districts 8 Apr 1956
maps.description: The 587 dispensary districts of Ireland at the census of 8 Apr 1956, mapped from the District Electoral Divisions the census report lists for each (CSO Census of Population 1956, Vol. 1, Table 10, which gives each district's DEDs by their 1911 reference numbers, read against the DEDs and acreages of Table 11). The DED map is Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's District Electoral Divisions in force on census day (Connacht 1919, Leinster 1954, Munster 1955, Ulster 1921). Every district carries a grade (confidence) and the reason for it (confidence_reason): A where the printed area equals the sum of its DEDs' areas in Table 11, so the composition is the census's own; B where the composition checks only as part of a group or needed a small adjustment; C where it could not be checked, for the reason given. 550 are graded A; 12 B, where Table 10 prints one bracketed area for a group (Cobh Nos. 1-2, Middleton Nos. 1-2, Rathkeale Nos. 1-2, Sligo Nos. 1-3, Enniscorthy North and South) or none (Annacotty, Clarina and Limerick Rural), and the group's DEDs add up to it exactly; and 25 C: the Dublin county districts and Waterford Rural Nos. 1-2, printed as registrars' districts partly in the county borough with no area, and districts in Kildare, Waterford and Galway that divide DEDs (each divided DED placed with the district holding its larger part, or by the best fit to the printed areas). Two pairs of Dublin districts with no whole DED of their own are shown together (Crumlin / Terenure; Finglas and Glasnevin Nos. 1 and 2), and Coolock and Drumcondra No. 2 is not a separate feature. The city dispensary districts of Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Waterford are not mapped: the census builds them from parts of DEDs and wards, so each county borough is shown as one unit, without a population. A district that crosses a county boundary is shown as one part per county, as the table prints it. Each district carries its census area, population, Table 10 reference numbers and DEDs; quote census_acres rather than the map area, which takes in lakes and estuaries the census leaves out. Population is printed for 581 of the 587.
maps.changeNote: Since 1951 the Cobh, Middleton, Rathkeale and Sligo dispensary districts were each divided along their registrars' districts (Cobh Nos. 1-2, Middleton Nos. 1-2, Rathkeale Nos. 1-2, Sligo Nos. 1-3), and Enniscorthy into North and South.

maps.description: The 575 dispensary districts of the Irish Free State at the census of 26 Apr 1936, mapped from the District Electoral Divisions the census report lists for each (CSO Census of Population 1936, Vol. 1, Table 10, which gives each district's DEDs by their 1911 reference numbers, read against the DEDs and acreages of Table 11). The DED map is Phelim Birch's and Paddy Matthews's District Electoral Divisions in force on census day (Connacht 1919, Leinster 1931, Munster 1921, Ulster 1921). Every district carries a grade (confidence) and the reason for it (confidence_reason): A where the printed area equals the sum of its DEDs' areas in Table 11, so the composition is the census's own; B where the composition checks only as part of a group or needed a small adjustment; C where it could not be checked, for the reason given. 572 are graded A, 1 B (North Dublin Rural, where a stray piece of the DED map is placed by adjacency) and 2 C (Droichead Nua and Kilcullen, which divide Ballysax East DED; it is placed whole in Kilcullen). The city dispensary districts of Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Waterford are not mapped: the census builds them from parts of DEDs and wards, so each county borough is shown as one unit, without a population. A district that crosses a county boundary is shown as one part per county, as the table prints it. Each district carries its census area, population, Table 10 reference numbers and DEDs; quote census_acres rather than the map area, which takes in lakes and estuaries the census leaves out.

maps.name: Dispensary Districts 18 Apr 1926
maps.description: The 582 dispensary districts of the Irish Free State at the census of 18 Apr 1926, mapped from the District Electoral Divisions the census report lists for each (CSO Census of Population 1926, Vol. 1, Table 10, which gives each district's 1911 Table VII DED reference numbers, its area and its 1926 population), drawn on Paddy Matthews's 1926 District Electoral Division map. The table was read from the page images and checked: persons equal males plus females in every row, the districts add up to every printed superintendent registrar's district and county total, and the district populations with the four city units add up to the state total of 2,971,992. The 1926 Table 11 is not held, so each printed area is checked against the 1936 Table 11 acreages of the district's DEDs: 570 districts are graded A (they agree within 0.2%), 10 B and 2 C. B: five Dublin districts whose DEDs the 1930 city extension redrew (both parts of Donnybrook, Rathmines, North Dublin Rural and Rathfarnham), checked against the map instead, and Killiney (0.24% out); and Tramore, Killenagh and Wells, Crossabeg and Wexford, which have their 1936 DEDs but a printed area 33 to 246 acres different (the DED acreages were revised between 1926 and 1936). C: Kilcullen and Newbridge, which divide Ballysax East DED (placed whole in Kilcullen). Each district carries its grade and the reason for it (confidence, confidence_reason). Several districts were later merged or redrawn and appear here as they were in 1926: Balleen (Urlingford), Finnea No. 1 and No. 2, Street No. 1 and No. 2, Scrabby No. 1 and No. 2, Ballyfarnan No. 1 and No. 2, Carrickbeg, Burt, Clonbrock and Killeroran, the Longford and Granard districts, the Birr districts of Offaly, the Galway districts of Clifden, Roundstone, Galway and Portumna, and the Dublin districts before the 1930 city extension; names are as printed in 1926 (Bagenalstown, Kells, Navan, Maryborough, Philipstown, Newbridge, Mountcharles, Binghamstown). The city dispensary districts of Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Waterford are not mapped: the census builds them from parts of DEDs and wards, so each county borough is shown as one unit, without a population. A district that crosses a county boundary is shown as one part per county, as the table prints it. Each district carries its printed 1926 population and area, its Table 10 reference numbers and its DEDs.

maps.name: Pobal HP Deprivation Index (2022, by Electoral Division)
maps.description: The Pobal HP Deprivation Index for 2022, by Trutz Haase and Jonathan Pratschke for Pobal, calculated from Census 2022, for the Electoral Divisions of the Republic of Ireland. Each ED is shaded by its relative index category. The relative score is scaled so that 0 is the national average: a lower (more negative) score is more disadvantaged and a higher score more affluent. The categories are Pobal's 10-point bands, from 1 'extremely disadvantaged' (below -30, darkest) through 'marginally below average' (-10 to 0) and 'marginally above average' (0 to 10) to 8 'extremely affluent' (30 and above, lightest). Clicking an ED shows the score, Pobal's label, the population and the census indicators behind the index (age dependency, lone parents, primary-only and third-level education, and male and female unemployment). The relative score compares each ED with the rest of the State in 2022 only, so it says which areas are more or less deprived than others, not how deprived an area is in absolute terms. It cannot be compared across years, and it cannot be compared with the Northern Ireland Multiple Deprivation Measure, which ranks areas on different indicators (there, rank 1 is the most deprived). The figures are drawn on Civgraph's 2022 Electoral Division map (eds-2022, the CSO census EDs: 3,420 mapped units, 30 of them groups of two or three EDs that the CSO publishes together, and three EDs drawn in two parts), matched to Pobal's own ED map by area. Every one of the 3,420 mapped units has a value; 3,408 overlap their Pobal unit by 90% or more, and the rest, a few city EDs, by at least 80%, the difference being the two maps' generalisation; every ED code also agrees with Pobal's. Source: Pobal HP Deprivation Index, Electoral Division 2022 (Pobal, https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=4f379645b4004151a28f3d62d299192d), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0); the same figures are in Pobal's "Deprivation Index Scores 2022" on data.gov.ie (https://data.gov.ie/dataset/pobal-hp-deprivation-index-scores-2022).
